prompt: In the `Week` component of this lesson, which line creates the object that holds `minutes`?

choices.text: None of them; Angular builds it
choices.why: Right. You hand the class over and the framework constructs it.

choices.text: `export class Week`, since exporting a class makes the instance
choices.why: That declares the class. Declaring it creates no object.

choices.text: `minutes = 165;`, the line that gives the field its value
choices.why: That is a field initialiser. It runs when an object is built, and something else builds it.

choices.text: `@Component({...})`, which turns the class into an object
choices.why: The decorator describes the class. It does not make an instance of it.

prompt: A colleague says Angular is a framework because it is bigger than React. What does this lesson say the difference is?

choices.text: Size: past a certain number of packages and features, any library becomes a framework
choices.why: Size is the wrong axis. A huge library is still something you call.

choices.text: The direction of the call: a framework calls your code, and decides when
choices.why: Right. That is the whole distinction, and size follows from it, not the other way round.

choices.text: TypeScript: a framework has types and a library does not
choices.why: Plenty of libraries are written in TypeScript. Types do not decide who calls whom.

choices.text: Whether it runs in the browser
choices.why: Both run in the browser. React does too.

prompt: Match each concern with the part of Angular that covers it, as the lesson's table lists them.

pairs.left: sharing objects between parts of the app

prompt: Which of these is a framework in the sense of this lesson, even though nobody calls it one?

choices.text: `Array.prototype.map`, because you pass it a function and it calls that function for you
choices.why: You call `map`, and it calls your function right then, inside your call. You never gave up the when.

choices.text: The browser, running your `addEventListener` function on a click
choices.why: Right. You handed over a function and the browser decides when it runs.

choices.text: `npm`, because it installs packages for you
choices.why: npm runs when you run it. Nothing of yours is called by it.

choices.text: `JSON.parse`, because it builds objects you did not write
choices.why: You call it and get the answer back. That is a library call.

prompt: An organisation moves developers between eight Angular teams every year. Which of Angular's properties pays off most for it?

choices.text: A smaller bundle than the alternatives, which saves bandwidth
choices.why: The lesson claims nothing of the sort, and lesson 2 measures an empty app with a real size.

choices.text: One way per concern, the same in every team
choices.why: Right. A person who changes team reads the new code on the first day.

choices.text: That each team can pick its own forms library
choices.why: That is the React situation the table describes, and it is the opposite of what helps here.

choices.text: Leaving TypeScript out of the smaller projects
choices.why: Every Angular project is TypeScript; there is no such option.

prompt: Angular supports each major version for how many months in total, active development and long-term support together?
Angular moved its templates from `*ngIf` to `@if` across codebases with thousands of files. What made that possible without every team rewriting by hand?

choices.text: The old syntax stopped compiling on the day of the release, which forced the change
choices.why: The lesson says the old forms kept working for several majors while teams moved.

choices.text: TypeScript rewrote the templates when it compiled them
choices.why: TypeScript checks types; it does not edit your files.

choices.text: Migrations: small programs, shipped with a release, that `ng update` runs to rewrite your code
choices.why: Right. An update edits the project where an API changed.

choices.text: A search and replace that the documentation asks each team to run
choices.why: That would be the manual work the migrations exist to avoid.

prompt: Where does this course install the Angular CLI?

choices.text: Globally, with `npm install -g`, so `ng` works in every folder
choices.why: The course installs nothing globally, so two projects can use two versions without meeting.

choices.text: Inside the project, at the exact version the project names
choices.why: Right. A second project next year can use another version.

choices.text: In `~/js-tools`, beside `page.mjs`
choices.why: That folder holds the browser tools. The CLI belongs to the project.

choices.text: In `~/.local/node`, next to Node itself
choices.why: That is where a global install would go, and the course avoids one.

prompt: You run the planner's dev server inside a virtual machine and open `http://localhost:4200` in the browser on your own desktop. Nothing loads. Why?

choices.text: The server listens on the guest's own `localhost`, which your desktop cannot reach
choices.why: Right. `localhost` means a different machine on each side.

choices.text: Angular does not run inside a virtual machine
choices.why: It does; the course was recorded in one.

choices.text: The browser on the desktop is a different version from the one `look` drives, and the page needs that one
choices.why: A different browser version would still load the page.

choices.text: Port 4200 is reserved by the operating system
choices.why: Nothing reserves it; the dev server picked it as its default.

prompt: `npx @angular/cli@22.2.4 version` printed a page of `EBADENGINE` warnings and then a refusal. Which program refused?

choices.text: npm, when it read the `engines` field
choices.why: npm only warned, and went on to install and run the CLI.

choices.text: Node, which cannot run code written for a newer version
choices.why: Node ran the CLI fine; the CLI read the version and stopped.

choices.text: The program npx started
choices.why: Right. Its message names the versions it accepts.

choices.text: The operating system, because the package needs a newer kernel
choices.why: Nothing in either message mentions the system.

prompt: Match each npm error code with what it says about the network.

pairs.right: the registry's name did not resolve

prompt: npm printed forty lines of error and ended with the path of a log file. Where does the lesson say to look first?

choices.text: The last line, because it is the most recent
choices.why: The last line is where the log is, which is rarely the cause.

choices.text: Near the top, after `npm error code`
choices.why: Right. The code and the lines after it name what went wrong.

choices.text: The log file, before reading anything on the screen
choices.why: The screen already carries the code; the log is for when it does not.

choices.text: The stack trace lines that start with `at`
choices.why: Those say where in npm's own code the error passed, which is npm's business.

prompt: `node hello.ts` printed `45 min` twice, although `label("45")` passes a string to a parameter typed `number`. Why did nothing complain?

choices.text: Node strips the annotations without checking them
choices.why: Right. Checking is the compiler's job, and `tsc` refused the same file.

choices.text: `"45"` is converted to a number before the call, so the types agree
choices.why: Nothing converts it: `"45" + " min"` is string concatenation.

choices.text: Strict mode is off by default in Node
choices.why: Strict mode is a JavaScript setting and has nothing to do with types.

choices.text: The annotation `: number` only applies to the return value
choices.why: `m: number` annotates the parameter; `: string` after the parentheses is the return.

prompt: What exit code did `npx tsc --noEmit --strict hello.ts` end with?
`sessions.find(...)` is typed `Session | undefined`. What does the compiler require before you read `.minutes` from the result?

choices.text: Nothing, because `find` always returns an element of the array
choices.why: It returns `undefined` when nothing matches, and the type says so.

choices.text: A cast written as `as Session` on every use
choices.why: A cast would silence the check rather than satisfy it, and the lesson does not use one.

choices.text: A check such as `if (next)` around the read
choices.why: Right. That is narrowing.

choices.text: An interface with `minutes?:` instead of `minutes:`
choices.why: That would make `minutes` optional on every session and solve nothing about `undefined`.

prompt: In `note?: string`, the question mark makes the property ___.
In `constructor(readonly label: string) {}`, what does `readonly` in front of the parameter do?

choices.text: Declares a field called `label` and fills it with the argument, and the field cannot be reassigned
choices.why: Right. That is a parameter property.

choices.text: Makes the argument a constant inside the constructor only
choices.why: It declares a field on every instance, not a local constant.

choices.text: Stops the caller from passing a variable, so only a literal string is accepted
choices.why: The caller may pass any string.

choices.text: Freezes the string so its characters cannot change
choices.why: Strings never change in JavaScript; `readonly` is about the field.

prompt: `sessions` in `Week` is `private readonly`. Which of these lines, written inside a method of `Week`, does the compiler accept?

choices.text: `this.sessions = [];`
choices.why: `readonly` forbids pointing the field at another array, even from inside the class.

choices.text: `this.sessions.push(s);`
choices.why: Right. The field is fixed; the array it points at is not.

choices.text: `delete this.sessions;`
choices.why: Deleting the field is a change to it, and `readonly` refuses changes.

choices.text: None of them, because `private readonly` makes the array immutable
choices.why: Neither word reaches inside the array.

prompt: `function first<T>(list: T[]): T | undefined` is called as `first(["git", "javascript"])`. What type does the result have?

choices.text: `T | undefined`, because T is only known at run time
choices.why: T is filled in at compile time, from the argument.

choices.text: `string`, since the list is not empty
choices.why: The type does not look at how many items there are, so `undefined` stays.

choices.text: `string | undefined`
choices.why: Right. T is `string`, and the function may find nothing.

choices.text: `any`, because generics switch the checks off
choices.why: Generics keep the connection between the argument and the result; nothing is switched off.

prompt: `node label.ts` failed with `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token` at the `@`. Why?

choices.text: The decorator has a type error that Node found
choices.why: Node checks no types at all.

choices.text: A decorator is syntax that Node 22 cannot run
choices.why: Right. The file has to be compiled by `tsc` first.

choices.text: `@Labelled` should have been written `@labelled`, in lower case
choices.why: The name is fine; the compiled version runs with it.

choices.text: Decorators only work inside an Angular project
choices.why: The compiled file ran under plain Node and printed its line.

prompt: Put what happened, when `out/label.js` ran, in order.
items: the function `Labelled("the planner")` returned the decorator
the decorator received the class `Planner` and printed its line

prompt: With today set to Friday 23 October 2026, how many minutes are planned in the planner's week?
hint: Monday to Sunday, the week that contains today.

prompt: Set today to Tuesday 27 October 2026 instead. Which sessions are in the week now?

choices.text: Sessions 2 to 5, as before, because the data did not change
choices.why: The week follows today, and the 27th starts a new week on Monday the 26th.

choices.text: Only session 6, on the 27th, its first Tuesday
choices.why: Right. The week runs from the 26th to 1 November, and session 6 is the only one in it.

choices.text: Sessions 5 and 6, the two that are not done
choices.why: Being done or not decides the second number, not which week a session is in.

choices.text: None, because the planner only counts sessions before today
choices.why: The week includes the days after today up to Sunday.

prompt: Which is true of a TypeScript type annotation once the application is running in the browser?

choices.text: It is checked again on every call
choices.why: Nothing checks it at run time; it is gone.

choices.text: It no longer exists: the types were erased when the code was compiled
choices.why: Right. That is why a server's answer can still surprise you, which lesson 12 returns to.

choices.text: It is kept as a comment, for debugging
choices.why: The compiled code carries no trace of it.

choices.text: It becomes a runtime `instanceof` test
choices.why: An interface has no runtime form for `instanceof` to test.

prompt: A team of two experienced React developers must ship a prototype in three weeks and throw it away after a trade fair. Which argument from this lesson applies to them?

choices.text: Angular's eighteen months of support, which protects the prototype after the fair
choices.why: The prototype is thrown away after the fair, so a support schedule buys it nothing.

choices.text: One way per concern, which helps them move people between teams
choices.why: Two people in one team move nowhere.

choices.text: The price of being called: Angular costs more before the first screen, which is what they are short of
choices.why: Right. The lesson says Angular suits less well a short-lived project for a team that already knows React.

choices.text: Migrations, which will update the prototype to Angular 22 for them
choices.why: There is no later version of a prototype nobody keeps.
